title: How a Bloom filter says “maybe”
dek: A Bloom filter stores a set as a handful of bits. It can say “maybe” to a word it never saw, but never “no” to one it did, and the number of hashes sets how often that “maybe” is wrong.

sections.heading: A set made of bits
paragraphs: Suppose you want to remember which words you have seen without storing the words. A Bloom filter starts with m bits, all 0. To add a word, you hash it k different ways, each hash picking one of the m bits, and set those k bits to 1. That is the whole write path: no words are kept, only bits.

To ask whether a word is in the set, you hash it the same k ways and look at its bits. If any of them is 0, the word was never added: *definitely not*. If all of them are 1, the word was probably added, but you cannot be sure, because other words may have set those bits. The filter's honest answer is *maybe*.

sections.heading: Watch it fill up
paragraphs: The figure has 32 bits and a list of twelve animal names. Drag n to add the first n animals, and change k, the number of hashes per word. Then pick a word to ask about. Arrows run from the word to its k bits.

Start with “cat”, which is in the set: all three of its bits are lit, and they always will be. Now ask about “plum”. One of its bits is 0, and that single 0 is proof. Then ask about “cherry”. You never added it, yet all three of its bits are 1: a false positive. At k = 3, “cherry” happens to land on exactly the same three bits as “fox”.

figure.title: Inserting words, asking about words
figure.caption: Each word is hashed k times and sets k of the 32 bits. Drag n to insert more animals, change k, and pick a word to ask about. Hatching marks a false “maybe”.
figure.alt: A row of 32 bits after inserting 8 animal names with 3 hashes each: 20 bits are set. Asking about “cat” finds all 3 of its bits set, so the answer is maybe; “plum” hits a 0 bit, so it is definitely not; “cherry” finds all 3 bits set though it was never added, a false positive.

sections.heading: Why “no” is always true
paragraphs: Bits only ever go from 0 to 1. Adding a word never clears a bit, so a word you added keeps all of its bits lit for good, and the filter can never answer “definitely not” about it. Every mistake runs one way: a word you never added finds all of its bits already set by others.

Ask about “hen”, the twelfth animal, and drag n up from 8. At n = 11 “hen” already says maybe, before you have added it: other animals set its bits. At n = 12 it is in the set for real. From the outside the two answers look the same, and that is exactly what “maybe” means. The figure can tell them apart only because it keeps the list; the filter cannot.

sections.heading: Predicting the false positives
paragraphs: You can predict how often “maybe” is wrong. Each of the k·n hashes misses a given bit with probability 1 − 1/m, so after n words a bit is still 0 with probability `(1 − 1/m)^(kn) ≈ e^(−kn/m)`. A word you never added is a false positive when all k of its bits are 1, which gives `FPR ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k`. For m = 32, n = 8 and k = 3 that is `(1 − e^(−0.75))³ ≈ 14.7%`.

The figure also measures. It asks about 50 fruits and vegetables it never added and counts how many come back maybe. At the defaults that is 10 of 50, or 20%, a little above the prediction. The formula describes an average filter. This one happens to have 20 of its 32 bits set rather than the expected 17, and `(20/32)³ ≈ 24%`. A filter this small is noisy; with more bits, the measured rate settles onto the formula.

sections.heading: Choosing k
paragraphs: More hashes cut both ways. Each extra hash is one more bit a stranger has to match, which helps, but it also fills the bits faster, which hurts. In the first figure at n = 8, the predicted rate is 22% at k = 1, 14.7% at k = 3 and 22% again at k = 6. Somewhere in between is a best k.

Setting the derivative to zero gives `k = (m/n)·ln 2`, the point where about half the bits are set. There the false-positive rate is `(1/2)^k ≈ 0.6185^(m/n)`. The curve below plots the rate against n for your m and k. The marker shows the n at which your k is the best choice, and the dotted curve is the best any k could do. Drag along the curve and watch it touch the dotted line at the marker.

figure.title: False positives as the filter fills
figure.caption: The curve is (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k for your m and k. The dotted line is the best any number of hashes could do; the marker shows where your k is the best choice.
figure.alt: Line chart of the false-positive rate against the number of items inserted, for 32 bits and 3 hashes: the rate rises from near 0 at 1 item to 14.7% at 8 items and 86% at 32 items. A dotted curve shows the best possible rate, which the line touches at about 7.4 items, where 3 hashes is optimal.

takeaway: A Bloom filter never says no to a word it holds, because bits only turn on. Its one error is a false “maybe”, at a rate near (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k, which is lowest when k ≈ (m/n)·ln 2 and half the bits are set.
